paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch began his speech trembling with nerves. Cold sweat stood on his forehead, and he felt hot and cold by turns all over his body. He described this himself afterwards. He regarded the speech as his _chef-d’œuvre_, the _chef-d’œuvre_ of his whole life, his swan song. He did die nine months later, of galloping consumption, so he really did have the right, as it turned out, to compare himself to a swan singing its last song. He had put his whole heart into that speech, and every bit of brain he had. And poor Ippolit Kirillovitch unexpectedly showed that he had some feeling, at least, for the public good and for “the eternal question” hidden away inside him. The real strength of his speech was its sincerity. He truly believed the prisoner was guilty. He was not accusing him merely as a duty of his office, and when he called for vengeance he trembled with a genuine passion “for the security of society.” Even the ladies in the audience, though they stayed hostile to Ippolit Kirillovitch, admitted that he made an extraordinary impression on them. He began in a voice that kept breaking, but it soon grew strong and filled the court until the end of his speech. As soon as he had finished, though, he nearly fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which are ominous for an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public a good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.

“One day we see a brilliant young officer of high society, at the very start of his career, murder in a cowardly, underhand way, without a pang of conscience, an official who had once been his benefactor, and the servant girl as well, to steal back his own I.O.U. and whatever ready money he could find on the man. ‘It will come in handy for my pleasures in fashionable society and for my career in the future.’ After murdering them, he puts pillows under the head of each victim, and goes away. Next, a young hero ‘decorated for bravery’ kills the mother of his chief and benefactor, like a highwayman. To persuade his companions to join him he claims that ‘she loves him like a son, and so she will follow all his directions and take no precautions.’ Granted that he is a monster, yet I do not dare say, in these days, that he is the only one. Another man will not commit the murder, but will feel and think as he does, and is just as dishonorable in soul. In silence, alone with his conscience, he asks himself perhaps, ‘What is honor, and is the condemnation of bloodshed not a prejudice?’

“Perhaps people will cry out against me that I am morbid and hysterical, that this is a monstrous slander, that I am exaggerating. Let them say so—and heavens! I would be the first to rejoice if it were so! Oh, do not believe me. Think of me as morbid, but remember my words. Suppose only a tenth, only a twentieth part of what I say is true—even so, it is awful! Look at how our young people take their own lives. They never ask themselves Hamlet’s question, what lies beyond. There is no sign of such a question in them, as though everything that concerns the soul and what awaits us after the grave had long since been wiped from their minds and buried under the sands. Look at our vice, and at our profligates. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the unlucky victim in the present case, was almost an innocent babe compared with many of them. And yet we all knew him; ‘he lived among us!’...

“Yes, one day perhaps the leading minds of Russia and of Europe will study the psychology of Russian crime, for the subject deserves it. But that study will come later, at leisure, when the whole tragic topsy-turvydom of our present time lies farther behind us. Then it can be examined with more insight and more impartiality than I am able to bring to it. For now we are either horrified, or pretend to be, while in truth we gloat over the spectacle. We love strong and eccentric sensations that tickle our cynical, pampered idleness. Or else, like little children, we brush the dreadful ghosts away and hide our heads in the pillow, so as to go back to our games and merriment as soon as the ghosts have vanished. But one day we must begin life in sober earnest. We must look at ourselves as a society. It is time we tried to grasp something of our social position, or at least made a start in that direction.

“A great writer[9] of the last generation compared Russia to a swift troika galloping toward an unknown goal. He exclaims, ‘Oh, troika, birdlike troika, who invented you!’ and adds, in proud ecstasy, that all the peoples of the world stand aside respectfully to let the recklessly galloping troika pass. That may be. They may stand aside, with respect or without it. But in my poor opinion, the great writer closed his book this way either out of childish, naïve optimism, or simply out of fear of the censors of his day. Suppose the troika were drawn by his own heroes, Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov. It could reach no rational goal, whoever might be driving. And those heroes belonged to an older generation. Ours are worse specimens still....”

At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch’s speech was interrupted by applause. The liberal meaning of this comparison was appreciated. The applause did not last long, it is true, so the President did not think it necessary to warn the public, and only looked sternly in the direction of the offenders. But Ippolit Kirillovitch was encouraged. He had never been applauded before! All his life he had been unable to get a hearing, and now he suddenly had a chance to reach the ear of all Russia.

“What, after all, is this Karamazov family, which has gained such an unenviable notoriety throughout Russia?” he continued. “Perhaps I am exaggerating, but certain basic features of the educated class of today seem to me reflected in this family picture. Only in miniature, of course, ‘like the sun in a drop of water.’ Think of that unhappy, vicious, unbridled old man who has met such a sad end, the head of the family! He was born noble, but began life poor and dependent. An unexpected marriage brought him a small fortune. He was a petty knave, a toady and a buffoon, with fairly good though undeveloped intelligence, and above all he was a moneylender, who grew bolder as he grew richer. The abject, servile side of him fell away, and what remained was a malicious, sarcastic cynicism. Spiritually he was undeveloped, and his vitality was excessive. Life held nothing for him but sensual pleasure, and he raised his children to see it the same way. As a father he felt no duties at all. He mocked the very idea of them. He left his little children to the servants, was glad to be rid of them, and forgot them completely. The old man’s maxim was _Après moi le déluge_. He stood for everything that is opposed to civic duty, for the most complete and malignant individualism. ‘Let the world burn, for all I care, so long as I am all right.’ And he was all right. He was content, and he was eager to go on living the same way for another twenty or thirty years. He cheated his own son. He spent the money that came from the boy’s mother on trying to win his mistress away from him. No, I do not intend to leave the prisoner’s defense wholly to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I will speak the truth myself. I can well understand how much resentment the father had piled up in his son’s heart.

“But enough, enough of that unhappy old man. He has paid the penalty. Let us remember, though, that he was a father, and one of the typical fathers of our day. Am I being unjust when I say he is typical of many modern fathers? Alas! Many of them differ from him only in not professing such cynicism openly. They are better educated and more cultured, but their philosophy is at bottom the same as his. Perhaps I am a pessimist, but you have agreed to forgive me. Let us agree beforehand on this: you need not believe me, but you must let me speak. Let me say what I have to say, and keep some of my words in mind.
“Now for the children of this father, this head of a family. One of them is the prisoner before us, and the rest of my speech will concern him. The other two I will touch on only in passing.

“The elder is one of those modern young men with a brilliant education and a vigorous mind who have lost all faith in everything. Like his father, he has already denied and rejected a great deal. We have all heard him, for he was a welcome guest in local society. He never hid his opinions. Quite the contrary. That justifies me in speaking rather openly of him now, though not, of course, as an individual, but as a member of the Karamazov family. Another person closely tied to this case took his own life here last night. I mean an afflicted idiot, once the servant and possibly the illegitimate son of Fyodor Pavlovitch: Smerdyakov. At the preliminary inquiry he told me, in hysterical tears, how the young Ivan Karamazov had horrified him with his spiritual audacity. ‘According to him, everything in the world is lawful, and nothing must be forbidden in the future. That is what he always taught me.’ I believe that idiot was driven out of his mind by this theory, though the epileptic fits he suffered from, and this terrible catastrophe, no doubt helped to unhinge his faculties. But he let fall one very interesting remark, which would have done credit to a more intelligent observer. That is really why I have mentioned it. ‘If there is one of the sons who is like Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it is Ivan Fyodorovitch.’

“With that remark I end my sketch of his character, since it would be indelicate to go further. Oh, I have no wish to draw any more conclusions and croak like a raven over the young man’s future. We saw today in this court that good impulses still live in his young heart. Family feeling has not been destroyed in him by lack of faith and by cynicism, which came to him more through inheritance than through any thinking of his own.

“Then the third son. Oh, he is a devout and modest youth, and he does not share his elder brother’s gloomy and destructive view of life. He has tried to hold on to the ‘ideas of the people,’ or to whatever goes by that name in certain circles of our intellectual classes. He held on to the monastery, and came within an ace of becoming a monk. It seems to me that, unconsciously and at so early an age, he has shown the timid despair that drives so many in our unhappy society. They dread cynicism and its corrupting influence, and they wrongly put all the mischief down to European enlightenment. So they go back to their ‘native soil,’ as they say, to the bosom, so to speak, of their mother earth. They are like frightened children, longing to fall asleep on the withered breast of their decrepit mother, and to sleep there forever, only to escape the horrors that terrify them.
